patches.old: 'Cities that have invested heavily in public transit have seen reductions in traffic congestion. Therefore, expanding public transit is the most effective strategy for reducing congestion.'
patches.new: 'Cities that have invested heavily in public transit have seen reductions in traffic congestion. Therefore, expanding public transit reduces congestion.'
patches.reason: The original conclusion claimed transit was the MOST effective strategy, a comparative leap the answer key did not cover — and one this lesson's own "Too Strong" section flags. Narrowing the conclusion makes the correlation-causation flaw the clear answer.

visual.title: Assumptions and functions
visual.alt: Left, five kinds of unstated assumption: causal, assuming A causes B when the evidence only shows co-occurrence; representativeness, one case standing for the whole; definitional, a contested term treated as settled; continuity, assuming what held before keeps holding; and value, one priority assumed to outweigh another. Below, the negation test: negate the candidate assumption, and if the argument collapses it is a real assumption. Right, the function taxonomy for why an element appears: support or illustration, concession or counterargument, qualification, contrast, analogy, transition, and establishing stakes. Below that, four traps: too strong, stated rather than assumed, out of scope, and distortion. A footer notes Reasoning Within the Text is about 30 percent of CARS and that function answers must name the element's role, not its subject.
visual.caption: An assumption is what the argument needs but never says.
